metric.why: Liquid-cooled AI racks with coolant, manifolds, and batteries are dramatically heavier than the enterprise racks most buildings were engineered for. Retrofit projects hit structural limits before electrical ones more often than the industry expected.
metric.definition: The structural weight the raised floor or slab supports per square foot, against the actual weight of installed racks.

reading.body:
Existing data center buildings hit structural weight limits before power limits when retrofitting for liquid-cooled AI racks, forcing expensive reinforcement or abandonment of floor space.

The industry designed raised floors and concrete slabs for enterprise servers weighing hundreds of pounds per rack. Liquid-cooled AI infrastructure adds coolant loops, manifolds, and battery systems that push individual racks toward or beyond a ton. A retrofit project discovers this constraint only after electrical and cooling systems are already planned, making it a hard stop rather than a parameter to optimize around.

This matters because it decouples AI scaling from the two constraints usually cited: power supply and electrical distribution. A data center can have available grid capacity and working cooling systems but still cannot deploy denser compute if the building's structure will not hold it. The metric tracks this directly as actual rack weight against the floor's rated load per square foot.

The data does not reveal how many existing buildings hit this limit, how often it occurs by geography or construction era, or what reinforcement costs relative to building total cost. It also does not cover newly constructed facilities built to specification. But it explains why some retrofit projects stall at the architectural phase, before power becomes the constraint.
